```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This file sits between `01_join_and_clean.Rmd` and `02_analysis.Rmd`. It
describes the data before any model is fitted: what the variables look like,
what is missing, and what the patterns are.

Every visual below states the question it is there to answer. A chart that
does not answer a question does not belong in the paper.

```{r load}
# patchwork is only used for the final side-by-side figure.
# install.packages("patchwork")   # run once in the console if needed
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

data <- read_csv("data_clean/analysis_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(data)
```


# Part 1: Where the data comes from

| Source | What I take from it | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| World Bank **Global Findex 2025** | Internet use by women and by men. Gallup surveyed adults aged 15+ in each country between May and December 2024, same question everywhere. | My independent variable |
| World Bank **World Development Indicators** | GDP per capita (PPP), female labour force participation, female secondary enrollment, overall internet use, urban share. Most recent value 2021–2024. | My three outcomes plus two controls |
| UNDP **Human Development Report 2025** | Gender Inequality Index, 2023. Higher means more unequal. | An extra control |

All three were downloaded and reduced by `00_download_sources.R` and joined on
ISO-3 country code in `01_join_and_clean.Rmd`. Nothing was edited by hand at
any point.



# Part 2: Summary statistics

```{r summary-table}
summary_table <- data %>%
  select(internet_women, internet_men, gap_diff, gap_ratio,
         gdp_pc_ppp, flfp, sec_enroll_fem_gross,
         internet_total, urban_pct, gender_inequality_index) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(
    n       = sum(!is.na(value)),
    missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    mean    = round(mean(value,   na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd      = round(sd(value,     na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    min     = round(min(value,    na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    median  = round(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    max     = round(max(value,    na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = c(
    "internet_women", "internet_men", "gap_diff", "gap_ratio",
    "gdp_pc_ppp", "flfp", "sec_enroll_fem_gross",
    "internet_total", "urban_pct", "gender_inequality_index"))) %>%
  arrange(variable)

knitr::kable(summary_table)
```



# Part 3: What is missing

```{r missing-count}
data %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing") %>%
  filter(missing > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(missing))
```

Which countries, specifically:

```{r missing-who}
data %>%
  select(country, gdp_pc_ppp, sec_enroll_fem_gross, gender_inequality_index) %>%
  pivot_longer(-country, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  filter(is.na(value)) %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(n_missing = n(),
            countries = paste(sort(country), collapse = ", "),
            .groups = "drop")
```

Three things to say about this:

- Female secondary enrollment is my weakest variable. 15 of 89 countries have
  no figure, which drops my enrollment models to n = 74.
- The missingness is not random. The countries without an enrollment figure
  are mostly lower-income, which means the enrollment results describe a
  slightly better-off subset of my sample.
- I did not impute anything. Every model simply uses the countries that have
  the variables it needs, and I report the n for each one.

## Visual 1: How big is the gap?

**The question:** how wide is the internet gender gap, and how much do
countries differ?

```{r fig-gap-hist, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
fig1 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = gap_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Most countries have a gap, but a few are extreme",
       subtitle = "Positive values mean men are further online than women",
       x = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)",
       y = "Number of countries") +
  theme_minimal()

fig1
```



## Visual 2: Which countries are at the extremes?

**The question:** where is the gap widest, and where are women actually ahead?

```{r fig-extremes, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
extremes <- bind_rows(
  data %>% slice_max(gap_diff, n = 10),
  data %>% slice_min(gap_diff, n = 5)
) %>%
  mutate(side = if_else(gap_diff > 0, "Men ahead", "Women ahead"))

fig2 <- ggplot(extremes, aes(x = reorder(country, gap_diff), y = gap_diff,
                             fill = side)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Men ahead" = "steelblue",
                               "Women ahead" = "darkorange")) +
  labs(title = "The ten widest gaps, and the five where women lead",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)",
       fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

fig2
```

Pakistan is an enormous outlier at 43.6 points.


## Visual 3: Is the gap worse where fewer people are online?

**The question:** does the gap shrink as a country gets more connected
overall? This matters because it is the reason I control for total internet
use later.

```{r fig-45, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.5}
fig3 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = internet_men, y = internet_women)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = region), alpha = 0.85, size = 2) +
  # Dark2 is colour-blind friendly, unlike ggplot's default palette
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "Women's internet use against men's",
       subtitle = "Dashed line is equality. Below it, men are further online.",
       x = "Men online (%)", y = "Women online (%)", colour = NULL) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

fig3
```




## Visual 4: Where is the gap concentrated?

**The question:** is the gap a regional phenomenon or spread evenly?

```{r fig-region, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5}
fig4 <- data %>%
  mutate(region = fct_reorder(region, gap_diff, .fun = median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = region, y = gap_diff)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "The gap by world region",
       subtitle = "Boxes show the middle half of countries; points are countries",
       x = NULL, y = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()

fig4
```


## Visual 5: The gap against each outcome

**The question:** before any controls, does the gap look related to my three
outcomes?

```{r fig-outcomes, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.6}
outcome_long <- data %>%
  select(country, gap_diff, log_gdp, flfp, sec_enroll_fem_gross) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(log_gdp, flfp, sec_enroll_fem_gross),
               names_to = "outcome", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(outcome = recode(outcome,
    log_gdp              = "Logged GDP per capita",
    flfp                 = "Female labour force participation (%)",
    sec_enroll_fem_gross = "Female secondary enrollment (%)"))

fig5 <- ggplot(outcome_long, aes(x = gap_diff, y = value)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Two slopes, and one flat line",
       x = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

fig5
```

GDP and enrollment slope down.
Female labour force participation is flat.


## Visual 6: The final figure

**The question:** what does the relationship between the gap and female labour
force participation look like once I hold overall internet use and
urbanisation constant?

A plain scatter of the two shows nothing. The added variable plot removes the
part of each variable that the controls already explain, and shows what is
left — which is the relationship the regression actually estimates.

```{r fig-final, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.4}
# none of these four columns has a missing value, so the residuals line up
# with all 89 rows of the data frame
plot_data <- data
plot_data$flfp_resid <- residuals(lm(flfp ~ internet_total + urban_pct,
                                     data = data))
plot_data$gap_resid  <- residuals(lm(gap_diff ~ internet_total + urban_pct,
                                     data = data))

panel_raw <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(gap_diff, flfp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey45") +
  labs(title = "Raw",
       subtitle = "No visible relationship (r = -0.05)",
       x = "Internet gender gap (percentage points)",
       y = "Female labour force participation (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

panel_adj <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(gap_resid, flfp_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Holding internet use and urbanisation constant",
       subtitle = "-0.65 points of participation per point of gap (p = 0.004)",
       x = "Internet gender gap (residual)",
       y = "Female participation (residual)") +
  theme_minimal()

fig6 <- panel_raw + panel_adj
fig6
```



# Part 5: Save the figures

```{r save-figs}
if (!dir.exists("figures")) dir.create("figures")

ggsave("figures/fig1_gap_distribution.png", fig1, width = 7,  height = 4,   dpi = 300)
ggsave("figures/fig2_extremes.png",         fig2, width = 7,  height = 5,   dpi = 300)
ggsave("figures/fig3_women_vs_men.png",     fig3, width = 6.5,height = 5.5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("figures/fig4_by_region.png",        fig4, width = 7.5,height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("figures/fig5_gap_vs_outcomes.png",  fig5, width = 9,  height = 3.6, dpi = 300)
ggsave("figures/fig6_final.png",            fig6, width = 10, height = 4.4, dpi = 300)

list.files("figures")
```

Also save the summary table, so the paper and the code never disagree.

```{r save-table}
if (!dir.exists("results")) dir.create("results")
write_csv(summary_table, "results/summary_statistics.csv")
```
